Match patterns in texts using spaCy

Source: R/spacy_match.R
spacy_match.Rd

Find the tokens that match patterns, using spaCy's rule-based matchers (see https://spacy.io/usage/rule-based-matching). A pattern describes either a sequence of adjacent tokens, or tokens that are connected in the dependency parse, wherever they are in the sentence: the verb of a passive clause together with its subject and its agent, for instance. A token is described by its attributes, which can be those that the language model assigns, such as the part of speech or the dependency relation. Words and phrases can be matched too, given as in quanteda: as a character vector, a quanteda::phrase() object or a dictionary, with wildcards or regular expressions according to valuetype. Every kind of pattern gives rows of the same table. Unlike the patterns given to spacy_initialize() as entity_patterns, these do not change the pipeline or the entities of a document.

Usage

spacy_match(
  x,
  pattern,
  valuetype = c("glob", "regex", "fixed"),
  case_insensitive = TRUE,
  overlap = c("longest", "all", "first"),
  n_process = 1L,
  batch_size = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

a character object, a quanteda corpus, or a TIF-compliant corpus data.frame (see https://github.com/ropenscilabs/tif)

pattern

the patterns to match. The first four kinds are lexical patterns, which describe tokens by their text and to which valuetype and case_insensitive apply, as in quanteda:

  • a character vector, in which each element describes one token, such as "tax*". The label of a match is the name of the element, or its text when it has no name; elements with the same name are alternatives for that label. An element is one token even when it contains a space, so "new york" matches nothing: give a sequence of tokens with quanteda::phrase().

  • a quanteda::phrase() object, or a list of character vectors, in which each element is a sequence of adjacent tokens, with one string for each token: phrase("new york*") is the same as list(c("new", "york*")). The strings are used as they are given, and are not tokenized by spaCy, so that they set the token boundaries: phrase("Acme , Inc.") describes three tokens. The label is the name of the element, or else its strings joined by a space.

  • a quanteda dictionary, which is converted with as_entity_patterns(), given valuetype and case_insensitive: the top-level keys are the labels. A value that has no wildcard (or any value, with valuetype = "fixed") is a phrase that spaCy tokenizes; a value with a wildcard, or a regular expression, is split at its spaces, with one part for each token.

  • the collocations found by quanteda.textstats::textstat_collocations(), each of which is a sequence of its words, labelled by the collocation. The words are matched as they are, as quanteda matches collocations: only case_insensitive applies, and a * matches a *. Use phrase() on the collocations to have them read according to valuetype.

The others are in spaCy's own structure, and set how they match themselves:

  • a named list, in which each name is the label of a pattern, and each element is a pattern in spaCy's structure. The names must be unique. An element is one of two kinds, and a list can hold both:

    • a token pattern, for a sequence of adjacent tokens: a list with one named list of attributes for each token, such as list(list(LOWER = "new"), list(LOWER = "york")). An element can also be a list of such token patterns, which are then alternatives for that label.

    • a dependency pattern, for tokens related in the dependency parse: a list of nodes, each a named list that describes one token, with RIGHT_ID, a name for the node, which labels the token it matches in the output; RIGHT_ATTRS, the attributes of the token as in a token pattern, such as list(DEP = "nsubjpass"), or an empty list() for any token; and, for every node but the first, LEFT_ID and REL_OP, the name of an earlier node and the operator that relates that node to this one, such as ">" when this node is a direct dependent of the earlier one. An element whose nodes have these keys is read as a dependency pattern. Each label has one dependency pattern: give alternative patterns labels of their own.

    Such a list can also hold character vectors, which are sequences as in a list of character vectors, and need no name.

  • a spacyr_entity_patterns object from as_entity_patterns(), whose labels become the labels of the matches. Patterns with the same label are alternatives for that label, and the IDs of the patterns are ignored. The object can hold phrases as well as token patterns; its phrases are tokenized by spaCy, and match exactly or in any case as the object says.

valuetype

how the strings of lexical patterns are read: "glob" (the default) for wildcards, where * stands for any number of characters and ? for one; "regex" for regular expressions; or "fixed" for exact matching, as in quanteda. Each string is compared with one token, and a glob or a fixed string must match the whole of it, while a regular expression can match any part. Regular expressions are those of Python's re module, not of R or of quanteda: "^\\p{L}+$", for instance, works in quanteda and is an error here.

case_insensitive

logical; if TRUE (the default, as in quanteda), lexical patterns match in any case.

valuetype and case_insensitive are an error when they are given and pattern holds no lexical pattern: only spaCy's token or dependency patterns, or a spacyr_entity_patterns object, whose phrases have their own case_insensitive.

overlap

which matches of sequences to return where matches of the same label overlap: "longest" (the default) keeps the longest of them, and of those of the same length the one that starts first; "first" keeps the one that starts first, and of those with the same start the longest; "all" returns every match, including those inside or overlapping another, as spaCy does. Matches of different labels can overlap whatever the value. It does not apply to dependency patterns, all of whose matches are returned: in a list that holds both kinds it applies to the token patterns, and it has no effect when pattern holds only dependency patterns, so that it can be given whatever the patterns are.

n_process

the number of processes for spaCy's nlp.pipe() to use: 1 (the default) processes the documents in the current R session's Python process, a larger number starts that many Python processes, and -1 uses all CPUs. Starting the processes and loading the model in each takes time, so more than one process helps only for large numbers of documents. A custom pipeline component must be defined in an importable Python module to be used in other processes.

batch_size

the number of documents that spaCy's nlp.pipe() processes together; NULL (the default) uses the pipeline's default (nlp.batch_size). Larger batches can be faster, but use more memory.

...

not used. An argument that is not one of those above is an error.

Value

A data.frame with the same columns for every kind of pattern, and no rows when nothing matches. A match of a sequence is one row. A match of a dependency pattern is one row for each node of the pattern, each of length 1, with the same match_id; two nodes can match the same token, which then has a row for each.

doc_id

the document

match_id

the number of the match within the document, starting at 1 in each document, so that doc_id and match_id together identify a match

label

the label of the pattern that matched. It does not say which of a label's alternative patterns matched, which spaCy does not report.

node

for a dependency pattern, the name of the node that the token matched, from RIGHT_ID; NA for a sequence

sentence_id, token_id

the sentence of the first token of the sequence, or of the node's token, and the position of that token in its sentence, both starting at 1 as in spacy_parse(). A sequence that crosses a sentence boundary is given the sentence of its first token. Both are NA when the document has no sentence boundaries, as when the pipeline has neither a parser nor a sentence segmenter.

text

the matched text: of the whole sequence, or of the node's token

start_id

the position in the document of the first token of the sequence, or of the node's token, starting at 1 and counting every token of spaCy's, as the rows of spacy_parse() do

length

the number of tokens: of the sequence, or 1 for a node

Rows are in the order of the documents in x. Within a document, matches are in the order of the start_id of their first row: the first token of a sequence, or the token of the first node of a dependency pattern. Of the matches that start at the same token, sequences come first, by length (the shortest first) and then by the order of the labels in pattern; matches of dependency patterns follow, by the positions of the tokens of their other nodes, taken in the order of the nodes, and then by the order of the labels. match_id numbers the matches of a document in that order, sequences and dependency matches together, and the rows of a dependency match are in the order of the pattern's nodes. The order does not depend on overlap.

Details

Patterns are matched against spaCy's tokens, and an attribute can only match when a component of the pipeline sets it: DEP needs the parser, for instance, and spaCy gives an error when the component is missing. Patterns that ask for an entity type (ENT_TYPE or ENT_IOB) give a warning when no component sets entities, as after spacy_initialize(entity = FALSE), since they then match nothing. The labels of tags and dependency relations differ between language models; spacy_parse(x, tag = TRUE, dependency = TRUE) shows those of the model in use. A match is only as good as the model's annotation of the text.

The values of spaCy's set operators (IN, NOT_IN, IS_SUBSET, IS_SUPERSET and INTERSECTS) can be vectors of any length, and whole numbers need not be integers, as for as_entity_patterns().

Lexical patterns are compared with spaCy's tokens, which differ from those of quanteda::tokens(): spaCy's English models split "U.K.-based" into three tokens, for instance. A string of a lexical pattern is one token, and matches only where spaCy made the same token: phrase("Acme, Inc.") asks for a token Acme,, which spaCy does not make, while phrase("Acme , Inc.") matches the three tokens of "Acme, Inc.". spacy_tokenize() shows the tokens of a text. spaCy also makes a token of a space that follows another space, which a pattern of a space matches. To match as quanteda does on the same tokens, with its regular expressions, apply quanteda::index() or quanteda::tokens_lookup() to quanteda::as.tokens(spacy_parse(x)).

A string without a wildcard is compared with the token's text or, with case_insensitive = TRUE, its lower case form (spaCy's ORTH and LOWER). A glob with a wildcard becomes a regular expression for the whole of that text or lower case form, in which a wildcard stands for any characters, including the newlines of spaCy's whitespace tokens. Lower case is spaCy's throughout, so that a pattern ignores case in the same way with a wildcard as without. A regular expression is applied to the token's text, with the flag (?i) when case_insensitive = TRUE.

The phrases of a spacyr_entity_patterns object, and dictionary values without a wildcard, are split into tokens by spaCy's tokenizer, and match the same sequence of tokens in a document, as described for as_entity_patterns(). They are matched with spaCy's PhraseMatcher, which stays fast for many thousands of phrases, as are the sequences of lexical patterns that have no wildcard or regular expression. A phrase that matches in any case, as dictionary values do, is tokenized as it is written, and spaCy's tokenizer can split the same word differently in another case: it keeps "Inc." as one token but splits "inc." into two, so the phrase "acme widgets, inc." does not match the text "Acme Widgets, Inc.", while the phrase "Acme Widgets, Inc." in any case does. A warning is given when a component of the pipeline, such as merge_entities, changes the tokens of the documents, since these phrases may then not match.

The operators in the REL_OP of a dependency pattern are spaCy's: among others, "A > B" when B is a direct dependent of A, "A < B" when B is the head of A, "A >> B" when B is anywhere below A, and "A . B" when B directly follows A; see https://spacy.io/usage/rule-based-matching#dependencymatcher for all of them. A dependency pattern can match many times in a sentence: a verb and any one of its dependents gives one match for each dependent. The pipeline needs a dependency parser, or another component that sets dependencies: when pattern holds a dependency pattern that relates nodes, a document that has no dependency parse is an error, rather than a document without matches.

Matching adds little to the time that parsing takes, except for many token patterns: a few thousand make it much slower, so give phrases as lexical patterns or phrases where you can, not as token patterns. Lexical patterns and dictionary values with wildcards or regular expressions are token patterns, but those of a single token are combined into one for each label. Patterns that need no entities are faster after spacy_initialize(entity = FALSE).

Kinds of pattern

What pattern can be, and which arguments apply to each kind:

patternMeaningLabelvaluetype, case_insensitiveoverlap
character vectoreach element describes one tokenits name, or else its textapplyapplies
phrase() object, or a list of character vectorseach element is a sequence, with one string for each token; the strings are not tokenized againits name, or else its strings joined by a spaceapply, to each stringapplies
quanteda dictionaryconverted by as_entity_patterns(): a value without a wildcard is a phrase that spaCy tokenizes, and one with a wildcard or a regular expression is split at its spacesthe top-level keyapplyapplies
collocationseach is a sequence of its words, matched as they arethe collocationonly case_insensitive applies; a valuetype other than "fixed" is an errorapplies
named list of spaCy token patternsa sequence of tokens described by their attributesthe namean error if givenapplies
spacyr_entity_patterns objectits phrases, tokenized by spaCy, and its token patternsits labelan error if givenapplies
named list of dependency patternsone token for each node, anywhere in a sentencethe namean error if givendoes not apply, and has no effect when there are no other patterns

A list can hold character vectors, token patterns and dependency patterns together; valuetype and case_insensitive then apply to its character vectors.

How each kind is matched:

Sequences of tokensDependency patterns
Matched by spaCy'sPhraseMatcher, for lexical patterns and dictionary values without a wildcard or a regular expression, and for the phrases of entity patterns; otherwise MatcherDependencyMatcher
Patterns for one labelany number, as alternativesone
n_process, batch_sizeapplyapply
Rows for one matchoneone for each node
The pipeline needsthe components that set the attributes asked for: only its tokenizer for lexical patterns and phrasesa dependency parse, in every document

Patterns of every kind are matched in one pass over the documents, so the texts are parsed once for a list that holds both token and dependency patterns.

Matches and quanteda

overlap = "longest", the default, chooses among overlapping matches as quanteda::tokens_lookup() does with its default, nested_scope = "key": no token is in two matches of the same key, and a value that lies inside a value of another key is a match for both keys. The two are equivalent when they start from the same candidate spans under the same keys, and then give the same number of matches for each key in each document. Applying tokens_lookup() to spaCy's tokens, quanteda::as.tokens(spacy_parse(x)), does not guarantee that. In particular:

  • A dictionary value without a wildcard is a phrase, which spaCy's tokenizer splits into tokens, while quanteda splits every value at its spaces. The value "Acme, Inc." matches the three tokens Acme, , and Inc. here, where tokens_lookup() looks for a token Acme, and finds nothing.

  • The values of a dictionary's nested keys are labelled here by their top-level key, which corresponds to tokens_lookup(levels = 1). Its default, levels = 1:5, reports nested keys such as place.us separately, and so also keeps matches of two of them that overlap.

A match is a distinct pair of doc_id and match_id, not a row: count those to count matches, since a match of a dependency pattern has a row for each node. With one row for each match, m1 <- m[!duplicated(m[c("doc_id", "match_id")]), ], the labels of each document are tokens as tokens_lookup() returns them: quanteda::as.tokens(split(m1$label, factor(m1$doc_id, levels = ids))). The levels ids are the identifiers of all the documents, which keep those that have no match: names(x) for a named character vector, sprintf("text%d", seq_along(x)) for an unnamed one, as.character(x$doc_id) for a data.frame with the columns doc_id and text, and quanteda::docnames(x) for a corpus. The "Rule-Based Matching" article shows the counts made from them.

quanteda::kwic() follows a different rule, which no value of overlap gives: it drops a match only when every one of its tokens is in another match, of any pattern. So it drops "New York" inside another label's "New York Times", which overlap = "longest" keeps, and keeps both of two matches of one label that partly overlap, of which overlap = "longest" keeps one. A concordance of the matches themselves, with kwic(index = as_index(m)), shows the matches that overlap kept: see as_index().

See also

as_entity_patterns() and spacy_initialize() to make matches named entities, and as_index() to show matches in their context with quanteda::kwic().

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
spacy_initialize()

txt <- c(doc1 = "The book was written by Jane. Jane wrote the book.",
         doc2 = "Mistakes were made, and the report is being rewritten.")

# words, with wildcards as in quanteda, in any case
spacy_match(txt, "writ*")
# labelled by their names
spacy_match(txt, c(WRITE = "*writ*", WRITE = "wrote", ERROR = "mistake*"))

# a sequence of tokens needs phrase(): a character element is one token,
# also when it contains a space, so the first of these matches nothing
spacy_match(txt, "the book*")
spacy_match(txt, quanteda::phrase("the book*"))
# the same, as a list of character vectors, with a label
spacy_match(txt, list(TITLE = c("the", "book*")))

# regular expressions, which are Python's
spacy_match(txt, "^(re)?writ", valuetype = "regex")

# matching case
spacy_match(txt, c("the", "jane"), case_insensitive = FALSE)
spacy_match(txt, quanteda::phrase("The book"), valuetype = "fixed",
            case_insensitive = FALSE)

# passive verbs, by the dependency and tag labels of the English models:
# a passive auxiliary, any adverbs or further auxiliaries, and a past
# participle
passive <- list(list(DEP = "auxpass"),
                list(DEP = list(IN = c("advmod", "neg", "aux", "auxpass")),
                     OP = "*"),
                list(TAG = "VBN"))
spacy_match(txt, list(PASSIVE = passive))

# adjectives before a noun: the longest match where matches of a label
# overlap, which is the default, or every match
adj_noun <- list(ADJ_NOUN = list(list(POS = "ADJ", OP = "+"),
                                 list(POS = "NOUN")))
spacy_match("A big red shiny ball.", adj_noun)
spacy_match("A big red shiny ball.", adj_noun, overlap = "all")

# two labels, the second with alternative patterns
spacy_match(txt, list(
  DET_NOUN = list(list(POS = "DET"), list(POS = "NOUN")),
  WRITE = list(list(list(LEMMA = "write")),
               list(list(LEMMA = "rewrite")))
))

# phrases that spaCy tokenizes, matched exactly or in any case
spacy_match(txt, as_entity_patterns(c(TITLE = "the book")))
spacy_match(txt, as_entity_patterns(c(TITLE = "the book"),
                                    case_insensitive = TRUE))

# a quanteda dictionary, with its wildcards
dict <- quanteda::dictionary(list(writing = c("writ*", "wrote", "the book"),
                                  error = "mistake*"))
spacy_match(txt, dict)
spacy_match(txt, dict, case_insensitive = FALSE)

# a dependency pattern for passive clauses: a past participle with a
# passive subject and a passive auxiliary as its dependents
clause <- list(
  list(RIGHT_ID = "verb", RIGHT_ATTRS = list(TAG = "VBN")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "verb", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "subject",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "nsubjpass")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "verb", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "aux",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "auxpass"))
)
m <- spacy_match(txt, list(CLAUSE = clause))
m

# one row for each match, with a column for each node
reshape(m[, c("doc_id", "match_id", "node", "text")],
        idvar = c("doc_id", "match_id"), timevar = "node",
        direction = "wide")

# token and dependency patterns in one list
spacy_match(txt, list(PASSIVE = passive, CLAUSE = clause))
} # }
